\title{When Shared Hyperparameters Reverse Model Rankings:\\A Controlled Study of Visual
Water-Condition Classification}

\author{\todo{author names, affiliations and ORCIDs before submission}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Comparisons between a custom architecture and pretrained baselines often reuse one training
configuration for every model. We show that this apparently controlled choice can
systematically favour the custom model. Using seven-class visual water-condition
classification as a case study, we evaluate ten architectures under an identical tuning
budget, five promotion seeds, and per-image predictions retained for every run. The
best-to-worst validation \mf{} spread within the same six-setting grid ranges from 0.032 for
the proposed AquaNet to 0.190 for ResNet-50, so a shared setting costs the most sensitive
baseline six times what it costs the proposed model. Moving from the shared setting to
per-model selection raises test \mf{} by 0.057 for ResNet-50 and 0.036 for EfficientNet-B0
but only 0.010 for AquaNet, and the resulting ranking places AquaNet ninth of ten, below a
top group of five that Holm-corrected paired tests cannot separate, and below its own
unmodified DenseNet-121 backbone. A balanced 54-run head\,$\times$\,MSRB\,$\times$\,CSAB
factorial with a parameter-matched neck control shows both proposed modules to be
null-to-negative. One positive result survives: removing the modules yields the lowest
uncalibrated expected calibration error of the ten models and a fitted temperature of 1.098,
significantly closer to the ideal $T\!=\!1$ than all nine others, at 7.61M parameters. After
temperature scaling that advantage disappears. We also find that a classifier reading only
file metadata reaches 0.69 accuracy against a 0.35 majority baseline, bounding what any
architecture on this data can claim. Together these results convert an apparent architecture
gain into a quantified evaluation-protocol effect and argue for equal tuning budgets rather
than equal hyperparameter values as the appropriate control.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
benchmarking, hyperparameter tuning, pretrained models, model calibration,
water-condition recognition, reproducibility, negative results
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ============================================================ 1
\section{Introduction}
Vision models are increasingly used to screen waterways from fixed cameras and drones,
complementing rather than replacing physical sensing~\cite{al2024drone,kim2023cctv}. In
parallel, architecture papers routinely compare a proposed network containing freshly
initialised layers against ImageNet-pretrained baselines. Giving every model the same
learning rate looks like the fair thing to do, yet it equalises a \emph{value} rather than
the \emph{opportunity} to find an appropriate value. A network that is almost entirely
pretrained and a network carrying several million randomly initialised parameters do not
occupy the same optimisation regime, and a single scalar cannot be neutral between them.

This study began as an attempt to validate AquaNet, a DenseNet-based network augmented with
a multi-scale residual block (MSRB), a channel--spatial attention block (CSAB), and an
optional hierarchical head. Under the original shared-hyperparameter protocol AquaNet
appeared to beat the baselines it was compared against. A diagnostic tuning grid reversed
that result. We treat the reversal as the finding rather than as an inconvenience.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item a controlled measurement of model-dependent hyperparameter sensitivity across ten CNN
and transformer configurations given an identical six-trial budget (\S\ref{sec:protocol});
\item a five-seed comparison under per-model validation selection, with paired tests, effect
sizes and Holm correction, showing the proposed model at rank nine of ten and the top five
statistically indistinguishable (\S\ref{sec:cnn}--\S\ref{sec:transformer});
\item a balanced 54-run head\,$\times$\,MSRB\,$\times$\,CSAB factorial with a
parameter-matched neck control, establishing a well-supported negative architecture result
(\S\ref{sec:ablation});
\item an evaluation across calibration, selective prediction, corruptions, out-of-distribution
transfer and explanation faithfulness, including one honest positive result for the stripped
architecture (\S\ref{sec:robust}); and
\item a shortcut analysis bounding how much of the task is solvable without pixel content at
all (\S\ref{sec:contribution}).
\end{enumerate}

We make no claim that RGB appearance measures physicochemical water quality. The task is
seven-class \emph{surface-condition recognition}, and no physicochemical parameter is
measured anywhere in this work.

% ============================================================ 2
\section{Related Work and Taxonomy}
\subsection{Architecture families evaluated}
The model set spans four convolutional generations --- residual~\cite{he2016resnet}, dense
connectivity~\cite{huang2017densenet}, mobile-efficient
designs~\cite{sandler2018mobilenet,tan2019efficientnet}, and the modernised
ConvNeXt~\cite{liu2022convnext} --- alongside the vision-transformer
lineage~\cite{dosovitskiy2021vit} and its two data-efficient descendants,
DeiT~\cite{touvron2021deit} and the hierarchical, window-attention Swin
Transformer~\cite{liu2021swin}. AquaNet's attention module follows CBAM's sequential
channel-then-spatial formulation~\cite{woo2018cbam}. Calibration analysis uses temperature
scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration}; saliency analysis uses Grad-CAM~\cite{selvaraju2017gradcam}
with deletion/insertion scoring.

\subsection{A taxonomy of ``fair comparison''}
Comparisons in the applied literature adopt one of three controls, and they are not
equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Equal values.} One learning rate, schedule and epoch budget for every model.
Cheap and reproducible, and the control this paper shows to be biased.
\item \textbf{Equal budget.} Every model receives the same number of tuning trials over the
same grid, each selecting on validation only. More expensive, and the control we advocate.
\item \textbf{Equal effort.} Each model is tuned until its author is satisfied. Common in
practice, unfalsifiable, and not reproducible.
\end{itemize}
Our concern connects to evidence that benchmark rankings shift with seeds and experimental
budgets~\cite{bouthillier2021variance,lucic2018gans}. We isolate a specific and directional
asymmetry: a shared learning rate advantages a custom head or neck carrying millions of new
parameters over a nearly fully pretrained baseline. The relevant unit of fairness is
therefore the search budget and the selection rule, not a common scalar.

\section{Dataset}\label{sec:data}
Three sets are used. \textbf{D1} is the primary in-distribution set of 2{,}799 images across
seven labels --- clean, algae, debris, foam, oil, turbid and uncertain --- with a fixed
1{,}956/416/427 train/validation/test split that is never resampled. \textbf{D2} contains 213
real video frames used only for adaptation. \textbf{D3} contains 146 held-out web and video
images used only for out-of-distribution testing. Table~\ref{tab:dataset} gives the
composition and Fig.~\ref{fig:dataset} the class, aspect-ratio and resolution distributions.

\textbf{Provenance and framing.} D1 originates from the public Kaggle collection
\texttt{vasundharadixit1826/real-and-ai-data} and contains AI-generated imagery alongside
photographs. It is therefore \emph{consolidated, audited and extended} here; it is not
introduced, named or released as a novel dataset, and this provenance limits every
ecological conclusion that could otherwise be drawn. \todo{confirm whether the Kaggle
account is co-author V.\ Dixit; if so, state the relationship in the data-availability
statement}

\textbf{Audit.} Exact MD5 duplicates were removed before splitting and no exact-duplicate
group survives. A perceptual-hash sweep at Hamming distance $\leq 5$ nevertheless retains 698
candidate cross-split pairs, which we report rather than remove because at that threshold the
set mixes genuine near-duplicates with distinct images of similar scenes. We do not claim the
splits are leakage-free. Section~\ref{sec:contribution} quantifies the consequence.

% ============================================================ 4
\section{Problem Formulation}
Let $f_\theta(x)$ map an image to a probability vector $p \in \mathbb{R}^7$. The primary
metric is the class-balanced
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{mF1}=\frac{1}{7}\sum_{c=1}^{7}\frac{2P_cR_c}{P_c+R_c},
\end{equation}
chosen over accuracy because the smallest class holds 24 test images and the largest 150.
All models minimise the same weighted cross entropy
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{c} w_c\, y_c \log p_c , \qquad
w_c = \frac{N}{7 n_c} \Big/ \overline{\left(\frac{N}{7 n_c}\right)},
\end{equation}
with the weights normalised to mean one so that class balancing does not also rescale the
effective learning rate. Validation \mf{}, never test performance, selects both checkpoints
and hyperparameters.

For model $j$ over the hyperparameter grid $\mathcal{H}$ we define protocol sensitivity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sens}
S_j=\max_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathrm{mF1}_{\mathrm{val}}(j,h)-\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathrm{mF1}_{\mathrm{val}}(j,h),
\end{equation}
the span a single shared setting can cost model $j$ within a budget every model receives
equally. Seed-matched comparisons use paired differences; family-wise error is controlled by
Holm's procedure within each metric.

% ============================================================ 5
\section{AquaNet Evolution}\label{sec:evolution}
The architecture reached its published form through a sequence of experiments whose protocol
we later found to be defective. We report both because the defects are the mechanism behind
the paper's finding.

Under that earlier protocol, on three-seed runs, AquaNet's flat variant reached 0.8463 test
\mf{} against 0.8292 for MobileNetV2 and 0.8277 for ResNet-50 --- an apparent lead over both
baselines then under comparison. Six defects were subsequently identified:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[D1.] checkpoints were selected on validation negative log-likelihood, which penalised
the higher-entropy AquaNet outputs far more than the baselines;
\item[D2.] baselines trained with focal loss while AquaNet trained with weighted cross
entropy;
\item[D3.] one learning rate served a nearly fully pretrained trunk and 3.5M freshly
initialised parameters alike;
\item[D4.] class balancing was applied inconsistently across arms;
\item[D5.] MSRB and CSAB were never tested underneath a working head, so module effects and
head effects were confounded; and
\item[D6.] per-image predictions were not retained, so no prediction-level test was possible
after the fact.
\end{enumerate}
Every subsequent result in this paper uses the repaired protocol of
\S\ref{sec:protocol}: one selection rule, one loss, separate parameter groups, class balance
applied once, head and neck as independent axes, and per-image predictions written for every
run. The earlier numbers are reported here for provenance only and are not comparable with
anything in \S\ref{sec:cnn} onward. Of the six defects, D3 is the one that grew into the
subject of this paper.

% ============================================================ 6
\section{Final Architecture}\label{sec:arch}
AquaNet-V3 combines a pretrained DenseNet-121 trunk with an MSRB, a CSAB, and either a flat
seven-way softmax head or a hierarchical head that factorises the label into a clean/%
contaminated decision and a contaminant type (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}, left). The full flat model
holds 10.53M parameters against 6.96M for the unmodified DenseNet-121 backbone, so the
proposed additions cost 3.57M parameters.

\begin{figure*}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{architecture.pdf}
\caption{Left: AquaNet-V3. MSRB and CSAB are ablated jointly and separately, and the head is
an independent axis. Right: the MatchedNeck control, which holds MSRB's parameter and
normalisation counts exactly while discarding its multi-scale structure.}\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{The MatchedNeck control.} MSRB contributes 3{,}407{,}872 convolution weights and
3{,}072 normalisation parameters. Simply deleting it therefore removes capacity and structure
together, and a resulting drop cannot distinguish ``multi-scale processing helps'' from
``3.4M more parameters help''. MatchedNeck (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}, right) is a single-scale,
undilated block matched to MSRB in parameter count, normalisation count and depth. It is the
control that makes the negative result of \S\ref{sec:ablation} interpretable, and it is the
reason that result is reportable at all.

Three configurations are carried forward: \emph{full} (flat head, MSRB on, CSAB on, the
published configuration), \emph{no-neck} (flat, both off), and \emph{hier} (teacher-forced
hierarchical head, MSRB on, CSAB off).

% ============================================================ 7
\section{Experimental Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
Inputs, splits, augmentation, loss, class balancing, epoch budget, early-stopping rule and
validation criterion are identical for all ten architectures (Table~\ref{tab:protocol}). Only
the learning rate and the backbone multiplier vary, and they vary through a procedure every
model receives equally.

\input{tables/protocol}

\textbf{Stage T: an equal budget, not equal values.} Each model receives the same six trials,
\begin{equation}
\eta\in\{10^{-4},\,3\!\times\!10^{-4},\,10^{-3}\},\qquad m_b\in\{0.1,\,1.0\},
\end{equation}
where $m_b$ multiplies the learning rate applied to the pretrained trunk relative to freshly
initialised modules. Each model's validation-selected pair is promoted to the five seeds
$\{7,21,42,1337,2024\}$. Phase 4 comprises 222 successful training runs in total, and every
headline run writes its per-image predictions.

We fix a single objective across all models rather than tuning the loss per family. Weighted
cross entropy was chosen once on validation and applied everywhere; alternatives such as
focal loss~\cite{lin2017focal} are implemented in the released code but were not used,
because varying the objective per model would reintroduce exactly the confound this study
exists to measure.

Table~\ref{tab:lr} reports what the identical grid produced per model. The selected settings
are not close to one another: ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B0 and all three AquaNet
variants select a backbone multiplier of 1.0, while ConvNeXt-T, DeiT-S and MobileNetV2 select
0.1, and the selected learning rates span an order of magnitude.

\input{tables/lr_selection}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{protocol_sensitivity.pdf}
\caption{Best-to-worst validation \mf{} spread $S_j$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:sens}) within the identical
six-trial budget. The three AquaNet variants are the three least sensitive models in the
study.}\label{fig:sensitivity}\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{sensitivity_grid.pdf}
\caption{The full six-trial grid. Each row is one model; the boxed cell is the trial it was
promoted from. The variation within a row is what a single shared setting risks.}
\label{fig:grid}\end{figure}

\subsection{The shared setting is not neutral}
Figure~\ref{fig:sensitivity} is the central measurement of this paper. Sensitivity ranges
from 0.0324 for AquaNet-full to 0.1901 for ResNet-50: the same fixed grid moves the most
sensitive baseline almost six times as far as it moves the proposed model. Seed-matched, the
move from the original shared setting ($\eta=3\times10^{-4}$, $m_b=0.1$) to per-model
selection is worth $+0.0574$ test \mf{} to ResNet-50, $+0.0356$ to EfficientNet-B0,
$+0.0143$ to DenseNet-121 and $+0.0136$ to MobileNetV2, but only $+0.0101$ to AquaNet-full;
ConvNeXt-T and DeiT-S are unmoved ($+0.0000$ and $-0.0002$), having already been near their
grid optimum. Every model that moved at all gained, and the proposed model gained least. That
ordering, not any individual value, is the finding.

The mechanism is direct. A nearly fully pretrained backbone needs conservative trunk updates
that are nonetheless not throttled to near-zero, whereas AquaNet carries roughly 3.5M new
parameters that need large updates. The shared setting was a reasonable compromise for a
model holding both kinds of parameter and a poor one for a model holding only pretrained
ones. A single shared learning rate is thus a model-specific choice wearing the costume of a
control.

% ============================================================ 8
\section{Classical Machine Learning Benchmark}\label{sec:classical}
Before comparing deep architectures it is worth establishing what generic colour and texture
statistics already achieve, because that bounds how much credit any architecture can claim.
We extract RGB and HSV histograms, local binary patterns at two scales, GLCM Haralick
descriptors and a coarse HOG, and fit logistic regression, a random forest, an RBF SVM and
gradient-boosted trees. The splits are the same, the class weighting is the same, and each
classical model receives the same six-trial tuning budget selected on validation \mf{} that
each deep model received in Stage T.

\input{tables/classical}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{classical.pdf}
\caption{Classical baselines on hand-crafted features against four deep models under the same
splits and the same tuning budget.}\label{fig:classical}\end{figure}

Hand-crafted features recover a large fraction of the task. The gap between the best
classical model and the best deep model is real but far smaller than the gap between either
and chance, which is the first indication --- developed in \S\ref{sec:contribution} --- that
much of D1's separability does not require learned representations.

\section{Convolutional Benchmark}\label{sec:cnn}
Table~\ref{tab:main} reports all ten finalists after per-model selection; we read the
convolutional rows here and the transformer rows in \S\ref{sec:transformer}.

\input{tables/main_ranking}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{ranking.pdf}
\caption{Tuned test \mf{} with 95\% $t$ intervals over five seeds. The dashed line marks
AquaNet-full, the published configuration.}\label{fig:ranking}\end{figure}

Among convolutional models ResNet-50 leads at 0.8798, followed by DenseNet-121 at 0.8751 and
EfficientNet-B0 at 0.8668, with MobileNetV2 last at 0.8425. The three AquaNet variants fall
between DenseNet-121 and EfficientNet-B0 --- hier at 0.8716, no-neck at 0.8701 --- with the
published full configuration at 0.8661, ninth of ten overall.

Two comparisons carry the section. First, AquaNet-full is below its own unmodified
DenseNet-121 backbone by 0.0090 \mf{} despite 3.57M additional parameters, so the proposed
additions do not pay for themselves on the metric they were designed to improve. Second,
ResNet-50 moves from last place under the shared setting to best convolutional model after
tuning; its position in the original comparison was an artefact of our configuration, not a
property of ResNet-50.

% ============================================================ 10
\section{Transformer Benchmark}\label{sec:transformer}
Swin-T is the validation-selected model at 0.9053 test \mf{}, ahead of DeiT-S (0.8871) and
ConvNeXt-T (0.8851, convolutional but included here as the modernised-CNN comparison point).
Table~\ref{tab:sig} reports paired seed-level $t$ tests of Swin-T against every other
finalist, Holm-corrected within each metric across nine comparisons.

\input{tables/significance}

\textbf{The top group is indistinguishable.} Swin-T's margins over DeiT-S, ConvNeXt-T,
ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 do not survive Holm correction on macro-F1
($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.303,\,0.303,\,0.303,\,0.175$). These five models form a group we cannot
separate at $n=5$, and we therefore do not claim that Swin-T is best; we report that it was
selected on validation and that its advantage over the top group is not established.

Swin-T does significantly exceed AquaNet-full ($\Delta=0.0392$, 5/5 seeds,
$p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0085$) and AquaNet-no-neck ($\Delta=0.0352$, 5/5,
$p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0199$). AquaNet-full's margin over the one model it beats, MobileNetV2,
is not significant.

Two statistical limits apply throughout and are stated once. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is
not reportable at $n=5$: its smallest attainable two-sided $p$ is 0.062 regardless of effect
size, so a non-significant Wilcoxon result would carry no information. Prediction-level
bootstrap and exact McNemar tests were computed from the retained per-image predictions, but
only for the seed shared by all configurations, and they are labelled as single-seed results
wherever they appear.

\section{Extensive Ablations}\label{sec:ablation}
The factorial crosses three heads (flat, hierarchical-naive, hierarchical teacher-forced),
three neck conditions (off, MatchedNeck, MSRB) and two CSAB states, at three seeds: a
balanced 54-run design over 18 cells. Fifteen further Stage-B runs are one-off sensitivity
experiments on a single cell and are reported separately below rather than averaged into the
marginals, because doing so would let one cell's side experiment move an axis it does not
belong to.

\input{tables/ablation_marginals}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{ablation_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cell means of the balanced 54-run factorial. No combination containing MSRB or CSAB
exceeds the cell with both switched off.}\label{fig:ablation}\end{figure}

Every marginal points the same way: MSRB off (0.8604) beats MatchedNeck (0.8537) and MSRB on
(0.8518); CSAB off (0.8586) beats CSAB on (0.8520); the flat head (0.8585) marginally leads
both hierarchical variants (0.8540, 0.8534).

\input{tables/matched_neck}

\textbf{The parameter-matched comparison.} Across 18 head-, CSAB- and seed-matched triplets,
MSRB scores $-0.0018$ \mf{} against MatchedNeck with 6/18 wins and $-0.0086$ against no neck
at all with 6/18 wins. MatchedNeck itself scores $-0.0068$ against no neck. The reading is
that the 3.4M additional parameters are mildly harmful in this position regardless of how
they are arranged, and that MSRB's multi-scale structure adds nothing on top of the capacity
it brings. Neither effect is large; both are consistently negative. The definitive tuned
five-seed comparison, AquaNet-full against AquaNet-no-neck, gives $-0.0040$ with 2/5 wins.
The modules are null-to-negative, not gains.

\textbf{Auxiliary sensitivity runs.} The 15 excluded runs sweep the hierarchical loss mixing
coefficient $\lambda_{\mathrm{mix}}$ and test an \texttt{uncertain}-exclusion variant of the
binary objective, both on the (hier-TF, MSRB on, CSAB on) cell only. Across
$\lambda_{\mathrm{mix}}\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}$ macro-F1 varies between 0.8451 and 0.8609
with overlapping seed spreads, giving no evidence that the mixing coefficient matters within
that range. At $\lambda_{\mathrm{mix}}=0$ the hierarchical objective is switched off entirely
while inference still routes through the binary\,$\times$\,type gating product, so neither
head receives a training signal and \mf{} collapses to $0.0247\pm0.0007$. That is a wiring
sanity check confirming the hierarchical path is genuinely in use, not a result about head
design, and we report it as such.

% ============================================================ 12
\section{Dataset Contribution Analysis}\label{sec:contribution}
How much of D1 is solvable without looking at the picture? We train a random forest on file
metadata alone --- width, height, aspect ratio, pixel count, file size, bytes per pixel and
the JPEG quantisation tables --- with no pixel content of any kind, and a second probe on the
mean and standard deviation of the three RGB channels.

\input{tables/shortcut}

The metadata probe reaches 0.6918 accuracy and 0.5822 \mf{} against a majority-class baseline
of 0.3513 and 0.0743. Six colour moments reach 0.7190 and 0.6099. Neither probe can see
water; both substantially exceed chance. The explanation is visible in the audit:
2{,}645 of 2{,}799 D1 images sit in a resolution group that spans more than one split, so
acquisition source is partially predictive of label and is distributed across the splits.

Two consequences follow, and both matter for reading every other number in this paper. First,
\emph{absolute} accuracy on D1 is inflated relative to any deployment in which source
identity carries no information about the label, and should not be transferred to one.
Second, the \emph{relative} ranking is unaffected: every model sees identical inputs and
identical splits, so the shortcut is available equally to all ten and cannot explain
differences between them. The protocol effect this paper measures is a difference between
models under a shared confound, not a product of it.

This also reframes \S\ref{sec:classical}. That hand-crafted colour and texture features come
close to deep models is consistent with a task in which a substantial share of the
separability is carried by low-level source statistics.

\section{Domain Generalization}\label{sec:ood}
D3 holds 146 images from sources disjoint from D1, between 14 and 26 per class. No D3 image
is used for training or selection at any point. D3 is a small held-out probe for measuring
transfer degradation; it is not a benchmark and we do not propose it as one.

\input{tables/ood}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\subfloat[Zero-shot ranking.]{\includegraphics[width=.50\columnwidth]{ood_transfer.pdf}}
\subfloat[D2 adaptation.]{\includegraphics[width=.47\columnwidth]{adaptation.pdf}}
\caption{Out-of-distribution evaluation on D3 (146 images). Error bars are one standard
deviation across seeds.}\label{fig:ood}\end{figure}

Every model loses roughly 40 points of \mf{} moving from D1 to D3. Swin-T leads at 0.5035,
followed by DeiT-S (0.4980) and ConvNeXt-T (0.4955). AquaNet-no-neck reaches 0.4787 while
AquaNet-full reaches 0.3957. The neck penalty grows from 0.0040 in distribution to 0.0829
out of it --- a factor of twenty --- which is the opposite of the generalisation rationale
that motivated the modules.

\input{tables/adaptation}

Fine-tuning on increasing fractions of D2 and re-testing on D3 raises \mf{} from 0.5318
zero-shot to 0.7069 with all 213 frames. The 75\% point (0.6456) falls below the 50\% point
(0.6653); with three seeds and 146 test images this ordering is not resolvable, and we claim
no monotone trend.

% ============================================================ 14
\section{Robustness and Calibration}\label{sec:robust}
\subsection{Corruptions}
Each test image is subjected to nine corruptions at five severities. Table~\ref{tab:robust}
gives the per-corruption degradations and Fig.~\ref{fig:corrupt} the full severity curves.

\input{tables/robustness}

\begin{figure*}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{corruption_curves.pdf}
\caption{Macro-F1 against corruption severity, mean over five seeds. Gaussian noise and
contrast are the most damaging; motion blur the least.}\label{fig:corrupt}\end{figure*}

DeiT-S is the most robust model (mean degradation 0.0255), followed by ConvNeXt-T (0.0315)
and Swin-T (0.0387). AquaNet-full and AquaNet-hier are the two \emph{least} robust models in
the study (0.0811 and 0.0843); removing the neck cuts AquaNet's degradation to 0.0479, better
than DenseNet-121, ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2. The modules make the model more brittle, not
less.

\subsection{Selective prediction and screening}
\begin{figure*}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{decision_quality.pdf}
\caption{Selective-prediction risk and mean corruption degradation. Lower is better on
both axes.}\label{fig:decision}\end{figure*}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{rc_curves.pdf}
\caption{Risk--coverage curves at seed 7.}\label{fig:rc}\end{figure}

Swin-T attains the best area under the risk--coverage curve (0.0104) and 0.9578 accuracy at
90\% coverage, against 0.0178 and 0.9333 for AquaNet-full. Treated as a binary screening
problem over 41 clean and 386 contaminated test images, DeiT-S achieves the lowest
false-clean rate (0.0135) --- the error that matters most for screening --- ahead of
ResNet-50 (0.0171) and Swin-T (0.0176); AquaNet-full is last at 0.0295. Swin-T's binary AUROC
is 0.9922 against 0.9769 for AquaNet-full. With only 41 clean images the specificity and
AUROC estimates carry wide intervals and should be read as indicative.

\subsection{Calibration: the one axis where removing the modules wins}
\input{tables/calibration}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{temperature.pdf}
\caption{Temperature fitted on validation, mean $\pm$ sd over five seeds, sorted by distance
from the ideal $T=1$. AquaNet-no-neck is the only model that does not require a large
confidence correction.}\label{fig:temperature}\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{calibration.pdf}
\caption{Left: expected calibration error before and after temperature scaling. Right:
reliability curves at seed 7; bins holding fewer than five images are omitted, and marker
area is proportional to bin count.}\label{fig:calibration}\end{figure*}

AquaNet-no-neck attains the lowest uncalibrated expected calibration error of the ten
architectures (0.0397 against 0.0528 for Swin-T) and requires a fitted temperature of 1.098,
where every baseline requires between 1.591 and 2.753 (Fig.~\ref{fig:temperature}). The gap
between AquaNet-no-neck and the second-closest model, DenseNet-121 at 1.591, is the largest
single margin anywhere in this study.

\input{tables/calibration_tests}

\textbf{What is and is not significant.} Testing distance from the ideal temperature,
$|T-1|$, pairwise across the five seeds, AquaNet-no-neck is closer to $T=1$ than
\emph{all nine} other models, on 5/5 seeds in eight of the nine cases, with Holm-corrected
$p\leq0.0276$ throughout (Table~\ref{tab:caltests}). That result is significant. The
uncalibrated ECE ranking is \emph{not}: the paired test of AquaNet-no-neck against Swin-T
gives $p=0.083$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.380$. We therefore state the ECE result as a ranking
over ten architectures and reserve the word significant for the temperature result.

\textbf{Three limits, all mandatory.} First, after temperature scaling the advantage
disappears: all ten models converge into 0.0301--0.0428 and Swin-T edges AquaNet-no-neck by
0.0003, a difference of no practical or statistical consequence ($p=0.89$). If a validation
split is available for fitting $T$, this result does not distinguish the models. Second,
AquaNet-no-neck is the less accurate model: 0.8701 test \mf{} against 0.9053 for Swin-T,
reported in the same table so the two rankings are never read apart. Third --- and this
pre-empts the obvious objection --- a merely timid model that hedged every prediction would
fit $T<1$. AquaNet-no-neck fits $T=1.098$, slightly \emph{above} one, so it is marginally
overconfident and near-ideal rather than underconfident. Low ECE here is not an artefact of
blunted confidence.

\textbf{Where this matters.} A canal-side camera has no held-out validation split in the
field, so $T$ cannot be fitted after deployment. A model shipping at $T\approx1.1$ is usable
as-is, whereas one needing $T\approx2.3$ reports roughly double the confidence it has earned.
We note this as a consideration, not a demonstration: no field trial was run and nothing in
this paper establishes deployment readiness.

\textbf{Ablation reading.} Removing MSRB and CSAB moves the fitted temperature from 1.640 to
1.098 and raw ECE from 0.0700 to 0.0397, both 5/5 seeds. Combined with
\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:ood} and the corruption results, the modules are not merely
null on accuracy --- they are actively harmful to calibration, to seed stability (mF1
standard deviation 0.0165 against 0.0069, 2.4$\times$), to corruption robustness and to
out-of-distribution transfer. Every axis we measured degrades when they are added.

\textbf{Measurement note.} Two independent ECE implementations exist in this codebase. They
agree to within $5\times10^{-4}$ on all ten models (Table~\ref{tab:ecesources}). All
calibration values quoted above come from the evaluation suite, the only source that also
carries the fitted temperature.

\section{Interpretability}\label{sec:interp}
Deletion and insertion scoring tests whether pixels ranked highly by Grad-CAM actually carry
the evidence the model uses: pixels are progressively removed (or added) in saliency order
and the predicted-class score is tracked.

\input{tables/explanations}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=.85\columnwidth]{explanations.pdf}
\caption{Deletion--insertion operating points, five-seed means over 256 images. Upper-left is
preferable.}\label{fig:explain}\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{gradcam_aquanet_seed42.png}
\caption{Representative AquaNet-full Grad-CAM panel at seed 42. Qualitative maps are
illustrative only; the deletion/insertion scores provide the faithfulness test.}
\label{fig:gradcam}\end{figure}

AquaNet-hier gives the lowest deletion AUC (0.7739) with insertion 0.9044, a gap of 0.1305;
ResNet-50 follows at 0.7747/0.8914. AquaNet-full's gap is markedly smaller (0.8304/0.8844,
gap 0.0540), so adding the modules also degrades the correspondence between saliency and
evidence. The three transformers occupy the opposite corner.

That last observation must be read with care and does not support a ranking. Gradient maps
are not architecture-neutral, and standard Grad-CAM is poorly matched to transformer token
mixing: the transformers' high deletion AUC is at least as likely to reflect the method's
mismatch as any property of the models. We treat these numbers as within-family diagnostics
only, and explicitly do not claim that AquaNet is more interpretable than Swin-T.

Model differences concentrate in the two smallest and hardest classes. Algae is nearly

in macro-F1, and the dominant confusion throughout is between \emph{clean} and
\emph{uncertain} in both directions. Because \emph{uncertain} encodes annotator
non-determination rather than a physical condition, part of the remaining error is label
ambiguity that no architecture can resolve.

% ============================================================ 17
\section{Discussion}
The ranking reversal has a simple mechanism and a general lesson. A nearly fully pretrained
backbone requires conservative trunk updates; a model carrying millions of fresh parameters
requires large ones. One shared scalar cannot serve both, and whichever model the shared
value happens to suit is advantaged by a decision presented as a control. Equalising the
search space and the selection rule exposes the asymmetry. It does not guarantee that the
globally best model is found --- a six-point grid measures local sensitivity, not the
optimum --- but it removes a one-sided advantage that is otherwise invisible.

The result also shows why ablations need parameter-matched controls. Deleting MSRB changes
capacity and structure simultaneously; MatchedNeck holds capacity fixed and still finds no
gain, which converts ``the module did not help'' from an ambiguous observation into a
supported claim. Without that control the same data would have been compatible with ``MSRB
helps but is under-parameterised''.

A negative architecture result is more credible when the same evaluation can detect a
positive one. It could here: the stripped variant is significantly closer to ideal
calibration than all nine alternatives. That the evaluation found a win where one existed,
on an axis nobody designed the modules for, is what makes the null findings elsewhere
informative rather than merely underpowered.

Practical guidance follows directly. Report the search space and the per-model selected
values. Give every model the same number of validation trials. Keep test data outside every
selection decision. Promote with multiple seeds and report the standard deviation. Save
per-example outputs so prediction-level tests remain possible afterwards. Correct for
multiplicity, and distinguish a ranking from a set of significantly separated models. For
deployment on data of this kind, the evidence supports choosing within the top group on
latency, memory and calibration grounds rather than selecting a custom architecture for
novelty.

% ============================================================ 18
\section{Limitations}
D1 is modest in size, publicly sourced and partly AI-generated; D3 contains only 146 images
with 14--26 per class. The test split holds 427 images, so accuracy differences are exact
multiples of $1/427=0.0023$ and small gaps should not be over-read.

Labels describe visible surface conditions, not chemical safety. No physicochemical parameter
is measured anywhere in this study, and no output should be used for drinking-water or
regulatory determinations.

Preprocessing resizes to $224\times224$ without preserving aspect ratio, and source aspect
ratios span 0.42--3.69. Source geometry therefore becomes a distortion cue. This behaviour is
retained in the released code, and documented there, because it is what produced the reported
results; it is a known defect, not a design choice.

We do not claim leakage-free splits. Exact duplicates were removed, but 698 candidate
cross-split perceptual near-pairs remain, and \S\ref{sec:contribution} shows that source
identity alone predicts the label well above chance. Absolute performance on D1 is inflated
relative to field conditions.

The tuning grid has six points. It measures local sensitivity, not exhaustive optimisation,
and a wider search could change individual placements within the top group --- though it
would have to reverse the direction of every per-model gain to overturn the paper's claim.
Five seeds is enough for paired $t$ tests but not for Wilcoxon; prediction-level tests exist
for one seed only. Only one task is studied, so the ranking-reversal mechanism should be
tested elsewhere before being assumed general. Grad-CAM comparisons across architecture
families are diagnostic only. No field trial was conducted and nothing here establishes
deployment readiness.

\section*{Ethics and Broader Impact}
Automated water screening can misdirect attention if its confidence is misread. The
calibration analysis in \S\ref{sec:robust} exists partly for that reason: a model reporting
double the confidence it has earned is worse than no model in a screening role. Predictions
from any system trained on this data must not be presented as measurements of water safety.

% ============================================================ 19
\section{Conclusion}
An apparent AquaNet advantage disappears under equal per-model tuning budgets. Shared
hyperparameter values penalise pretrained baselines up to six times more than they penalise
the custom network, and correcting for this reverses the ranking: AquaNet falls to ninth of
ten, below a statistically indistinguishable top group and below its own backbone. A balanced
factorial with a parameter-matched control shows its two proposed modules to be
null-to-negative on accuracy and actively harmful to calibration, seed stability, corruption
robustness and out-of-distribution transfer. Removing them yields the one positive result in
the study --- the lowest uncalibrated calibration error of ten architectures and a fitted
temperature significantly closer to ideal than all nine alternatives --- which disappears
once a validation split is available for temperature scaling.

The general lesson is precise: controlled comparisons should equalise tuning
\emph{opportunity}, not force unlike models to share an optimisation setting.

and all figure- and table-generation scripts are available at \todo{Zenodo DOI, minted from

Kaggle upload and its licence governs redistribution. The manifests permit exact split
reconstruction from the original source without redistribution. Every number in every table
and figure of this paper is recomputable from the released JSON files without a GPU and
without the images.
